rationale: RealMM is dominated by the hot matrix-multiply kernel Mm (478 of 903 text bytes) whose inner loop executes O(n^3) iterations, while the remaining functions (rInitmatrix, rInnerproduct, main, _start) run cold. I therefore set cost weights as tolerances: cheap, semantics-preserving passes (SUB, SPLIT, IGV) get high RuntimeCost/SizeCost/CorrectnessRisk tolerances so they apply broadly, including inside Mm, giving baseline resistance at negligible benchmark cost; IGV is weighted up because this program's state (the matrices) lives in globals that rInitmatrix/rInnerproduct/Mm share, so hiding global-variable structure pays off across the whole program. Expensive control-flow passes are throttled: BCF gets the lowest RuntimeCost tolerance (0.2) so opaque-predicate insertion is pushed off the hot kernel, and FLA similarly (0.3) since Mm's loop structure is simple and flattening it would cost dispatch overhead per iteration while adding little; both remain available for cold functions where their high SecurityGain (0.8/0.7) can be exploited for free. IBR and ICALL sit in the middle: indirection frustrates static call/branch recovery but each indirect branch or call costs on the hot path, so moderate tolerances let the selector use them selectively. Size weights are uniformly lenient because the binary is tiny (903 text bytes) and code-size overhead is a non-issue here; correctness is protected by never giving any pass a maximal tolerance, keeping riskier transformations gated by per-function risk features.
